# SSH Remote Server Setup

project URL: https://roadmap.sh/projects/ssh-remote-server-setup


We need to set up and organize access to our remote server so that it is practical, efficient, and secure.

## Step by step: key pair generated by the cloud provider

- If you created a remote server on a cloud provider, it probably suggested at that moment the creation of an SSH key pair for remote access and the definition of a rule to allow port 22 through the firewall for your IP address.

- With the key pair created, the public key will be attached to your remote instance. Download the private key to your machine, a good place to save it is `~/.ssh/keys/`.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.ssh/keys
mv ~/Downloads/key-pair.pem ~/.ssh/keys/
```

- Change the access permissions of your private key so that only the owner can read it, others and the group have no read permission.

```bash
chmod 400 ~/.ssh/keys/key-pair.pem
```

- At this point it is already possible to access the remote instance with the command below, where the `-i` flag identifies the key, the *ubuntu* is the user defined when the remote instance was created, the `@` is the "at" (such user is at such address), and the public IP of the instance.

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/keys/key-pair.pem ubuntu@203.0.113.10
```

- We can add an alias to this instance to make access easier, adding the remote instance information to the SSH configuration file on your machine. Use a text editor to copy the structure.

- In `~/.ssh/config`, add the text below replacing each line with the items that match your instance:

```ssh-config
Host server
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/keys/key-pair.pem
    IdentitiesOnly yes
```

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Host` | Alias name |
| `HostName` | Public IP or public DNS of the instance |
| `User` | User used to connect |
| `IdentityFile` | Private key used in the connection |
| `IdentitiesOnly` | Uses only the declared key, without trying others |

- Protect the configuration file, with read and write permission only for the owner:

```bash
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/config
```

- Now you can connect using only the `server` alias, like this:

```bash
ssh server
```

## Step by step: key pair generated locally

- We will use the `ssh-keygen` utility to generate our key pair for SSH, one public key and the other private. The public one you can share with platforms and remote servers, and the private one you will keep safe on your machine.

- Where the `-t` flag defines the encryption algorithm, `-C` defines a comment that will help find the key faster, and `-f` the path where the key will be generated.

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "test@email.com" -f ~/.ssh/keys/test
```

- When you run the command, it will ask if you want to create a **passphrase**: a password that protects the private key. Even if the file is stolen, it cannot be used without it. Always use it on personal keys and keep the passphrase in a safe place so you don't forget it.

```text
Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
Enter same passphrase again:
Your identification has been saved in /home/isadora/.ssh/keys/test
Your public key has been saved in /home/isadora/.ssh/keys/test.pub
The key fingerprint is:
SHA256:mjeMGiAsDf045RboygUtzPjfXFxIFXyZvtsJzvCfZ+A test@email.com
```

- Read permission only for the owner:

```bash
chmod 400 ~/.ssh/keys/test
```

- Now we will send the newly generated key to the remote server, using the `ssh-copy-id` utility, which copies the public key to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` with the correct permissions on the destination. Using the `server` alias, authentication is done with the first key, which is already configured:

```bash
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/keys/test.pub server
```

- With that we can already access the remote server with the new private key.

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/keys/test ubuntu@203.0.113.10
```

- Or create a new alias in `~/.ssh/config`, with your favorite text editor.

```ssh-config
Host server-2
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/keys/test
    IdentitiesOnly yes
```
- There you go, enjoy your new alias!

```bash
ssh server-2
```
